title: The Animals Become Helpers
subtitle: Each prince spares a mother animal

learningObjectives.text: How do the princes earn the animals' help?

helpers.work: Fairy Tales From Far and Near
helpers.author: Katherine Pyle
helpers.locator: Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals; Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals, normalized characters 561-1681
helpers.excerpt: The eldest Prince was about to shoot at her, but the bear cried out, “Do not shoot, Prince, and I will give you my three cubs for servants, one for you, and one for each of your brothers.” To this the Prince agreed. He let the bear go away unharmed, and the three cubs followed after the three Princes, each one behind his own master. After they had gone a bit farther into the forest, they saw a lioness, and she also had three young ones with her. Now it was the second Prince who was about to shoot, but the lioness called to him, “Do not slay me, Prince, and I will give my three cubs to you and your brothers, one to each of you.” Thereupon the Prince allowed her to go unharmed and the three young lions followed after the Princes with the bear cubs. Soon after that they saw a mother fox, and three little ones were with her. This time it was the youngest Prince who would have shot, but the fox called to him, imploring him to spare her life and offering instead her three young ones to the Princes. She too was allowed to escape, and now each Prince had a young fox, a young lion and a young bear to follow him.
helpers.note: Verbatim text from Katherine Pyle's 1922 English children's retelling. The collection labels it Lithuanian but does not identify an oral informant or underlying source text.

narrativeBlocks.title: Kindness on the road
narrativeBlocks.body: On their wanderings the princes meet creatures in need — a starving wolf, a wounded bear, a hare, a fox — and where food or help is asked, they share what little they have.

narrativeBlocks.title: The debt that waits
narrativeBlocks.body: Each kindness is a note held by the wild: the bear, the wolf, the hare — the animals promise or simply remember, and the tale will call them in.

narrativeBlocks.title: A kingdom of allies
narrativeBlocks.body: By the tale's midpoint, the youngest prince has a private army: the beasts of the field and forest owe him, and animal gratitude in the fairy-tale is stronger than steel.

narrativeBlocks.title: The helpers arrive
narrativeBlocks.body: When the impossible task comes — the dragon, the trial, the locked tower — the animals come in their turn: the bear's strength, the wolf's speed, each creature's own gift paid back.

narrativeBlocks.title: The kindness-mechanism
narrativeBlocks.body: This is the fairy-tale's oldest engine: a kindness to a small creature is never wasted. In this Lithuanian tale, the whole quest runs on accumulated animal debts.

quiz.prompt: How do the princes earn the animals' loyalty?

choices.text: By rescuing the animals from a trap
By swearing an oath at the forest's heart
By sharing what little they have with creatures in need — a kindness the animals repay
By freeing a captive king of beasts

quiz.explanation: Kindness is the coin — spent small, repaid large.

quiz.prompt: What do the animal helpers bring to the quest?

choices.text: Each creature's own gift — the bear's strength, the wolf's speed — paid back at the critical moment

quiz.explanation: The debt of the wild is paid in each creature's strength.
